items.title: OGP : le syndicat salue les 18 mois de gestion de l’ex-DG Aladji Cellou
items.description: À l’occasion de la cérémonie de prise de fonction et de passation de service organisée à l’Office guinéen de publicité (OGP), marquant l’arrivée de Mohamed Banks Bangoura à la tête de la direction, la section syndicale de l’institution, par la voix de son secrétaire général, est revenue sur les actions menées par l’équipe sortante, dirigée par Aladji Cellou Camara. Des initiatives qui, selon elle, ont contribué à redresser la situation de l’établissement et à redonner le sourire aux travailleurs de cette structure chargée de piloter et de coordonner les activités publicitaires en République de Guinée. S’exprimant au nom de l’ensemble des travailleuses et travailleurs qui font vivre, jour et nuit, l’Office guinéen de publicité, Mohamed Charles Kolié a saisi cette occasion pour saluer le bilan et les acquis concrets de la direction sortante. Selon lui, au cours des dix-huit mois de gestion de l’équipe précédente, des efforts remarquables ont été consentis en faveur du bien-être du personnel. « L’histoire retiendra notamment le paiement régulier des salaires, l’apurement des arriérés de 2024, le versement des cotisations à la CNSS, la location d’un immeuble moderne de six étages et l’amélioration de notre logistique de terrain avec deux pick-up et des motos neuves. Pour ces sacrifices consentis en faveur de notre stabilité, nous disons un grand merci. » S’adressant aux nouveaux responsables, le secrétaire général de la section syndicale a souligné que leur nomination à la tête de l’OGP suscite de fortes attentes au sein du personnel. Il a notamment insisté sur la nécessité d’une collaboration étroite entre les dirigeants et les travailleurs afin de consolider les acquis et de relever les défis à venir. « Au nom des travailleurs, je tiens à vous lancer un appel solennel du cœur : le personnel de l’OGP exige de ses leaders une collaboration étroite, une complicité professionnelle totale et une union sacrée absolue. » Dans la même dynamique, Mohamed Charles Kolié a exhorté le nouveau directeur général et son adjoint à cultiver une entente cordiale, estimant que la cohésion au sommet de la hiérarchie constitue un facteur déterminant pour le développement de l’institution. « L’histoire de cette maison a trop souffert des guerres intestines et des divisions au sommet qui ont fini par paralyser l’entreprise. Monsieur le Directeur général, vous apportez votre expertise émérite en communication et votre vision stratégique ; Monsieur le Directeur général adjoint, vous maîtrisez les rouages profonds de notre administration et les réalités du personnel. Vos forces sont complémentaires. Soyez un bloc uni, un tandem soudé et sans fissure, car c’est de votre entente que naîtra la prospérité de l’OGP. » Afin de permettre à la nouvelle équipe dirigeante de mieux appréhender les défis liés à la gestion des ressources humaines, la section syndicale a également tenu à présenter la situation des effectifs placés sous sa responsabilité. « Notre effectif global se compose de 145 employés permanents bénéficiant d’un contrat à durée indéterminée (CDI), 174 jeunes recrues de la promotion 2022 dont la situation contractuelle demeure, à ce jour, irrégulière, deux fonctionnaires titulaires détachés et sept agents extras qui appuient nos opérations. » Dans la perspective d’une amélioration durable des conditions de travail et d’une meilleure prise en compte des préoccupations du personnel, la section syndicale a officiellement soumis à la nouvelle direction un cahier de doléances articulé autour de cinq revendications majeures. « 1. La normalisation dans un bref délai de la situation des 174 recrues de 2022 : après quatre années de loyaux services et de résilience au sein de l’institution, ces jeunes cadres méritent et exigent l’obtention de leur contrat CDI. La revalorisation salariale des 145 employés en CDI, dont les traitements actuels demeurent dérisoires face au coût de la vie. La correction des disparités salariales et des injustices de traitement qui continuent de causer des frustrations légitimes parmi le personnel concerné. L’octroi de formations et de bourses à l’étranger, afin de renforcer nos capacités internes et de donner à nos équipes les armes techniques pour atteindre les objectifs de notre Plan stratégique 2030. L’institutionnalisation du dialogue social interne comme unique créneau de règlement des litiges, afin d’éviter les crises, les cris et les bruits extérieurs qui ont tant contribué à ternir l’image de notre société par le passé. » Pour conclure son intervention, le secrétaire général de la section syndicale de l’OGP a évoqué le parcours récent de l’institution, marqué par le départ de deux anciens directeurs généraux, limogés puis conduits en prison depuis 2021. « L’histoire récente de l’OGP nous impose de vous parler avec franchise et courage. Depuis 2021, deux de nos anciens directeurs généraux ont été limogés et conduits en prison. Cette instabilité n’honore pas la réputation de notre institution. C’est pourquoi nous vous demandons une vigilance de chaque instant contre le virus du favoritisme, de l’injustice et de la complaisance, qui ont toujours attiré le malheur et causé la chute de vos prédécesseurs. Notre ambition pour votre duo est immense : nous souhaitons qu’au terme d’une gestion saine, votre réussite commune vous propulse ensemble vers des promotions encore plus hautes au sein de l’État », a-t-il formulé. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article OGP : le syndicat salue les 18 mois de gestion de l’ex-DG Aladji Cellou est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Conakry : le procureur général ordonne le démantèlement des lieux criminogènes
items.description: Le procureur général près la Cour d’appel de Conakry, Fallou Doumbouya, a requis le concours des forces de sécurité pour identifier et démanteler les lieux servant à la préparation, à la commission ou à la dissimulation d’infractions dans la capitale. Dans une réquisition aux fins de concours de la force publique publiée à cet effet, il a instruit le commandant de la Gendarmerie spéciale de la ville de Conakry et le directeur régional de la Police de Conakry de procéder sans délai aux opérations nécessaires, en coordination avec les procureurs de la République compétents. Les opérations visent notamment les zones et abris criminogènes, les bâtiments, terrains et chantiers délaissés, utilisés à des fins délictueuses, les lieux de recel ainsi que les points de trafic, de vente ou de consommation illicites de stupéfiants et de substances psychotropes. Pour faciliter la localisation de ces sites, les forces de sécurité devront également solliciter l’appui de l’administration territoriale, notamment des conseils communaux et de leurs démembrements. La réquisition prévoit par ailleurs de faire cesser les infractions constatées, de démanteler les dispositifs affectés aux activités illicites et de procéder au déguerpissement des lieux concernés. Les personnes contre lesquelles existent des éléments individualisés de participation aux faits, en qualité d’auteur, de coauteur ou de complice, devront être identifiées. Leur interpellation et leur déferrement devant le procureur de la République compétent pourront intervenir, lorsque les conditions légales seront réunies. Le procureur général exige enfin que ces opérations soient menées avec un recours à la force strictement nécessaire et proportionnée. Les autorités concernées sont également tenues de lui rendre compte des diligences accomplies. La réquisition s’appuie sur l’article 41 de la loi L/2016/060/AN du 26 octobre 2016 portant Code de procédure pénale.

items.title: Loi de finances 2027 | Faible appui à la relance économique
items.description: Tout en saluant la proposition incluse dans le projet de loi de finances pour 2027, qui prévoit la création de nouvelles lignes de financement destinées à soutenir les startups et les petites entreprises, Yassine Gouiaa, président de l’Organisation nationale des entrepreneurs, a toutefois estimé que cette mesure demeure insuffisante. Lors de son intervention jeudi 22 octobre 2022, sur Diwan FM , M. Gouiaa a exprimé son étonnement face à l’absence, dans ce projet de loi, de mesures visant à soutenir les entreprises existant depuis plus de cinq ou dix ans. Il a par ailleurs estimé que le montant alloué à la relance économique, soit environ 230 millions de dinars, incluant une enveloppe de 35 millions de dinars dédiée aux seules sociétés communautaires qui peinent à exister, est dérisoire et insuffisant, surtout compte tenu de la crise actuelle et du renchérissement du coût de l’énergie ; il a, à cet égard, appelé à sa révision. Alors que ce texte affiche l'ambition d'atteindre un taux de croissance de 3,1 % pour l'année 2027. «Des lignes de financement avaient été approuvées dans le cadre de précédentes lois de finances, mais, à ce jour, les textes réglementaires nécessaires à leur mise en œuvre n'ont toujours pas été publiés» , a-t-il relevé. I. B. L’article Loi de finances 2027 | Faible appui à la relance économique est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: State counsel cross-examines prosecution witnesses in security breach case against Imaan, Hadi
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A state-appointed counsel on Friday cross-examined all prosecution witnesses in a security breach case against lawyers Imaan Zainab Hazir-Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha. Imaan and her husband, Hadi, are facing a jail trial in a 2024 case pertaining to the alleged disruption of an international cricket team’s security route and incitement to public unrest. The couple, accused of removing barriers from the route, was indicted on Oct 7. Anti-terrorism court Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra presided over the hearing held inside Adiala jail on Friday, during which state counsel Atif Mehmood cross-examined a prosecution witness. On Saturday, the court will provide Imaan and Hadi with questionnaires under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to record their statements. In a hearing on Thursday, the court appointed Mehmood as the state counsel to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses, replacing Taimoor Janjua, who was dismissed over his past conduct. The court had ruled to appoint the state attorney after the defence counsel failed to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses. During the last hearing, Imaan informed the court that she and Hadi did not need a state counsel as they already had their own lawyers. Hadi explained that their lawyers were frequently occupied with other cases at the Islamabad High Court (IHC), while the trial court had scheduled daily hearings at Adiala, making it difficult for them to attend every proceeding. The court had directed the prosecution witnesses to appear again on Friday, affirming that the cross-examination would proceed without further delay. Imaan and Hadi’s rearrest The lawyer couple has been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca) in the controversial social media posts case. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On Sept 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the Supreme Court suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and Hadi were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties).

items.title: El ‘todo vaquero’ de Pedro Sánchez en ‘La Revuelta’: diseccionamos el polémico atuendo del presidente
items.description: La aparición de Pedro Sánchez en La Revuelta dio anoche a Broncano el récord de su historia, con más de 33% de share de audiencias, y también un par de lecciones básicas de semiótica que no por antiguas dejan de ser interesantes. Frente a la crispación, que el político sonría y se muestre relajado, que incluso haga chistes o se meta en temas en los que nunca veríamos a un presidente, como la vida sexual o una celebración de sus propios memes. Y, confirmando el cliché político de que, en principio, la derecha es más dada al traje y la corbata para mostrar cierto orden de despacho, que Sánchez apareciera con vaqueros pitillo y camisa remangada del mismo material. El full denim (doble vaquero) no es nuevo en él: ha tirado de estilismos parecidos en su visita a La Palma o en otros programas como El Hormiguero, en 2023, donde acudió con una camisa vaquera que, si no era la misma que la de anoche, era exactamente igual. Durante esa misma campaña, eso sí, acudió a Ana Rosa con americana y camisa blanca sin corbata: por aquel entonces El Hormiguero era todavía un programa en el que el invitado venía a divertirse y al de Ana Rosa, no tanto. items.title: Why Trump Can’t Sell Putin a Deal
items.description: On April 7, 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson gave a speech at Johns Hopkins University in which he effectively offered to build the equivalent of the Tennessee Valley Authority for North Vietnam on the condition that Hanoi cease supporting the insurgency in South Vietnam. On the helicopter ride back from the speech, Johnson leaned across to an assistant, put his hand on his knee, and said of Ho Chi Minh, the North Vietnamese leader, “Old Ho can’t turn that down, Old Ho can’t turn that down.” Ho did turn Johnson down. Today, the incident is taught in political-psychology courses to illustrate how presidents can naively think that transactional politics, commonplace in states and cities, will work on the global stage, only to find out that nationalism, ideology, and rivalry matter more. Donald Trump has fallen into the same trap with Vladimir Putin, apparently believing that the right economic incentives will persuade the Russian leader to make peace. This approach is not working. Instead, it’s closing off the one realistic pathway to end the conflict with Ukraine, and making the war likelier to expand and worsen. Early in his second term, Trump was surprised that Putin would not end the war quickly with a freezing of the territorial lines and a promise that Ukraine would not join NATO. Rather than seeking to improve Ukraine’s position on the battlefield or apply leverage against Russia through sanctions, Trump decided to convince Putin that peace would be financially rewarding. Trump pulled his Ukraine envoy, Lieutenant General Keith Kellogg, off the negotiating team after the Kremlin complained that he was too favorable to Ukrainians and replaced him with his friend Steve Witkoff, a real-estate tycoon. The Russian financier Kirill Dmitriev would be Trump’s conduit to Putin. [ Robert F. Worth: The magician of the Kremlin ] Witkoff and Dmitriev worked out a deal almost a year ago that included a full lifting of sanctions, joint U.S.-Russian business ventures, and even Russia’s readmission to the G7 (turning it into the G8), but it foundered on Putin’s demand that Ukraine cede territory on the battlefield. Witkoff and Dmitriev continued their efforts. The latest version emerged in the past week as U.S.-Ukraine relations reached their lowest point since the Oval Office bust-up in February 2025. Trump and Putin struck an agreement in which Russia would provide diesel fuel to the United States and global markets. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky slammed the arrangement, saying that it was “not fair and honest” and that it looked like “a happy-birthday present for Putin.” An infuriated Trump called for Zelensky to be replaced and said that he was harder to deal with than Putin. In the days that followed, Kyiv accused Washington of curtailing intelligence cooperation, including by withholding information on incoming ballistic-missile strikes (the administration denied this). The Financial Times reported that the administration is considering returning some of the frozen assets to Russia as an incentive for a partial cease-fire. Trump then waived sanctions on Russia under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, saying that doing so was in the national interest of the United States. On Truth Social, Trump posted that he was in negotiations to end the war and didn’t “want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” As U.S.-Ukrainian relations seemed to nose-dive, the administration tried to convey a larger rationale behind its decision making. A senior official told The Washington Post ’s David Ignatius that because a Ukraine deal was proving difficult to negotiate, the White House would enlarge the problem and negotiate a regional deal. This would include provisions to supply energy to Europe through a new pipeline, with profits to be shared between Ukraine and Russia, and the resolution of Moscow’s differences with European countries. This proposal is, in effect, the Johnson plan. The naivete behind it would perhaps be excusable if Putin were a new leader with no track record, but he is a known quantity. Ukraine is his obsession, his white whale. He wants to subjugate it and has proved that he will pay an enormous price to achieve this goal. The immediate diplomatic problem that Trump needs to solve is that Putin will not settle for anything less than the surrender of additional territory by Ukraine, which is something no Ukrainian leader can accept. Putin stands little chance of taking this territory by force: The front line is largely static, thanks to the saturation of the area with drones. However, the Russian leader has two hopes. One is to break Ukraine this winter with a brutal air offensive that would destroy its energy grid and deliver misery to millions. Maybe such pressure would cause Ukraine’s front line to collapse or lead Kyiv to accept Moscow’s demands at the negotiating table. The other prospect is to escalate Russia’s shadow war against Ukraine’s European partners. Moscow is already linked to assassination plots, arson, and the planting of explosive-laden drones in airports. A number of European leaders, including Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and French President Emmanuel Macron, have warned that Russia is considering hitting Eastern European states with drone and missile attacks that it would later deny. Putin hopes that this shadow war will weaken European governments and bring to power parties that will cut off aid to Ukraine and pressure it to capitulate to Russia’s demands. [ Read: Russia’s real strategy in Europe ] If Putin succeeds in these two gambits—weakening Ukraine over the winter while stoking unrest in Europe—he will be confident that Russia can grind out a bloody victory over the next couple of years. Putin seems to think that time is on his side. Trump’s concessions reinforce that perception. But if Trump can change Putin’s expectations about the future, a diplomatic deal might become possible. In particular, Trump must convince Putin that the war will not get any better for Russia, and that the deal he can get now is better than the one he can get later. This means doing everything possible to ensure that Ukraine survives Putin’s winter campaign: supplying Kyiv with as much air defense as possible, providing advance warning of incoming missiles, encouraging allies to seize Russia’s sovereign assets to provide Ukraine with economic relief, and helping Ukraine impose costs on Russia. It also means helping Europe deter Putin from escalating his shadow war against NATO members. This is difficult but doable. Europe needs to convince Putin that increased attacks, especially any that result in casualties, will deepen Europe’s and the United States’ involvement in the Ukraine conflict. For instance, Europe could say that if Russia launches missiles or drones against NATO members, a European coalition will place air defenses in western Ukraine. Trump could tell Putin that if Russia keeps harassing Europe, he will clear the way with Elon Musk for Ukraine to use Starlink to hit military targets inside of Russia. If one of Russia’s attacks resulted in mass casualties, such as the downing of a civilian airliner, the allies could designate Russia a state sponsor of terrorism. When I served at the National Security Council in the Biden administration, we communicated this to the Russians after they plotted to place flammable devices on airliners carrying DHL packages. We made clear that such a designation would likely lead to the closure of the Russian embassy in the United States. They stopped the plots. Helping Ukraine survive the winter and deterring Russian attacks on Europe will help keep diplomacy alive. But to close the deal, Trump needs to convince Putin that his window of opportunity is closing. Here, Trump’s political weakness could work to his advantage. Putin surely fears that Trump’s successor—if a Democrat or a Republican other than J. D. Vance—will be more favorable to Ukraine. A new administration will likely increase U.S. support for Ukraine and rebalance any deal made in the Trump years, possibly linking sanctions relief to Russian withdrawal from all of Ukraine. Trump could turn this prospect into leverage. He can tell Putin that the opportunity for a favorable deal is real, but that it may not last forever. Only he can deliver it. If Putin keeps fighting, he will not make territorial gains, Ukraine will survive and retain the capacity to strike inside of Russia, Europe will become more involved, and the favorable terms will expire. Then Trump needs to get serious about revising the offer so that it is acceptable to Ukraine. At a minimum, that means a freezing of the territorial lines, and no legal recognition of the occupied territory. Trump wants to be remembered as the president who ended the war in Ukraine, but unless he changes course, he may instead be remembered as the president who gave Putin the confidence to widen and prolong it. Trump has spent nearly two years trying to convince Putin that peace will be more rewarding than war. To get a cease-fire, he must now convince him that war will be more costly than peace.

items.title: The Party That Must Not Be Named
items.description: F or most of the past two decades, Ohio Democrats have hobbled home in defeat on Election Day, beaten and battered in a state that used to be a national bellwether. In 2024, Donald Trump ran up an 11-point margin, while Sherrod Brown lost his seat in the Senate. But earlier this month, I found Brown campaigning at Ohio State University, his red L.L.Bean fleece blending in with the students’ scarlet-and-gray apparel. It was the last day for Ohioans to register to vote. “O-H!” Brown said. The students’ response came automatically: “I-O!” they screamed. Maybe they could try “O-H … I- vote ,” Brown suggested with a smile. It didn’t quite catch on. After blowing a 20-point lead against Texas early in the college-football season, the Buckeyes have turned things around—and Democrats are clearly looking to borrow more than a chant from their playbook. Beating a Republican Party that has dominated the state for the past two decades, they believe, requires speaking directly to voters’ frustrations. Brown, in particular, has focused his campaign on reminding everyone how terrible things are, and is betting that tapping into Ohioans’ anger—spurred by a combination of high prices , an unpopular war, and a flailing president—might just be enough to return to the Senate. Less than two weeks from Election Day, there are signs that the strategy may be working. Most polls show Brown and Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor—a first-time politician and physician who served as director of the Ohio Department of Health during the first few months of the coronavirus pandemic—leading or tied with their GOP rivals. At Ohio State, Brown’s cheery greeting was prelude to a bleak speech about the future that awaits young Ohioans. The 73-year-old warned that life would be much harder for these students than it was for him when he graduated (Yale, but he went on to earn two master’s degrees from Ohio State) five decades ago. “The system’s rigged,” he began, then listed all of the ways that young people are screwed: Corporations make more money than ever. Their CEOs earn hundreds of times more than the average worker. The dream of homeownership might be entirely out of reach for young Americans. Normal people, Brown kept repeating, just cannot get ahead anymore. Brown was telling a group of ambitious students at the state’s top-ranked public university that they don’t have a future—or at least not the future they want. And they were captivated. Afterward, when Brown chatted with them individually, some looked like they were talking to a therapist. Freshman Trent Carson told me he’s already afraid that he won’t be able to find a good job when he graduates. He also worries that his cousins, who are truck drivers, will be out of work if the price of diesel remains near record highs. Josie Speakman, the pink-haired College Democrats president who introduced Brown, voiced a similar pessimism. “It feels like we can't get ahead, despite working harder than ever,” she said. The system is broken, she said, but Brown is going to fix it. Brown’s speech lacked rhetorical flourishes; he spoke to the students in his signature rasp, offering no major ideas beyond pledging to end the Iran war and get rid of tariffs. Barack Obama he is not, except that Brown is the only Democrat besides Obama to win statewide political office in Ohio since 2006. Brown’s project this year is not to fix Democrats’ tattered image in the state; in fact, Brown seems determined not to remind anyone that he’s a Democrat unless he absolutely has to. His campaign ads target the incumbent, Jon Husted, for taking money from Jeffrey Epstein’s benefactors and supporting AI data centers that raise Ohioans’ electric bills. They do not mention Brown’s party affiliation. Nor does his campaign website. “In large swaths of Ohio, and the country, the Democratic Party’s reputation has become toxic,” Brown wrote in The New Republic last year. Not that Brown’s political identity is a secret. Husted, who was appointed to the Senate last year by Ohio Governor Mike DeWine after J. D. Vance became vice president, was in elementary school when Brown was first elected to the Ohio legislature. It was the same year Richard Nixon resigned the presidency. Brown is following the same approach that gave Trump three consecutive victories in Ohio: lean into voters’ grievances and convince them that voting for him is a way to fight back against the rotten status quo. It doesn’t matter if Ohioans think that Democrats are lousy too, so long as they vote for this one candidate who just so happens to be a member of the party. One Republican strategist told me that in Brown, a candidate who is well known and well liked, Republicans face a formidable opponent amid a terrible political environment for the party. “People obviously do not feel better economically,” the strategist, whose organization did not authorize him to speak publicly about campaign dynamics, said, “so they’re taking it out on us.” In 2024 , Brown was also leading in the polls just weeks before the election, and then lost the Senate seat he had held for nearly two decades to now-Senator Bernie Moreno. So what’s different this year? Brown’s answer is simple: Everything has gotten worse. Life got more expensive. Washington got more corrupt. And because he’s no longer an incumbent, he can somewhat more convincingly claim to be an outsider. “The system’s more rigged than it was,” Brown told me during an interview with a group of reporters after the Ohio State event. “My message hasn’t changed.” Republicans have responded by attempting to both validate voters’ concerns and suggest that things aren’t as bad as they seem. Ohio Republican Party Chair Alex Triantafilou, a lawyer from the Cincinnati suburbs, is spending the final weeks of the campaign traveling the state in a rented white minivan. Gas prices now average $4.07 per gallon in Ohio, down from $4.48 a month ago, after the legislature approved a 90-day gas-tax holiday— a policy proposed by Acton that Republicans adopted and repackaged into a victory for her Republican competitor, Vivek Ramaswamy. [ Read: Vivek Ramaswamy’s appalling campaign ad ] “I think if there’s any part of the Iran war that poses an issue for voters, it might be with gas prices, but we’ve solved that here in Ohio,” Triantafilou told me this month at a coffee shop near Columbus. He had driven more than 100 miles from Cincinnati that morning for a couple of meetings and was about to turn around and head back. He said he doesn’t think Ohioans are going to vote on how much it costs to fill up their tanks and considers the issue of affordability to be overstated by the media. The stock market is up, he pointed out. Husted made a similar argument in a pep talk earlier this month to conservative activists going out to canvass in Delaware County, on the northern fringes of Columbus. “We have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate in our history,” Husted told reporters before the canvassing event. “We made progress.” He sought to remind voters that inflation was worse a few years ago, when Joe Biden was president and Brown was in the Senate. Husted is no MAGA warrior. When he spoke to supporters at a barbecue on a farm near Athens recently, he earnestly asked attendees to call loved ones daily until the election and remind them to vote. A former collegiate Division III defensive back, Husted once turned down an opportunity to coach college football, and he still looks like someone who’d rather be outside tossing a ball around. At a rally in Youngstown last week, Trump was captivated by Husted’s athletic past. “I looked at his ass,” Trump said with admiration, “and then I looked at his hands. Look at his hands. He’s got these, like, claws. And I got it, you are a great athlete.” [ Read: All the president’s hotties ] It was Trump’s second time in Ohio in as many weeks. In a midterm election, when turnout tends to be lower, getting Trump’s biggest fans to go to the polls is the way to win, Ohio Republicans told me. They’re banking on that remaining true, despite the president’s broad unpopularity. “I understand the national environment sucks. In the other states, there are gonna be blue waves,” Michael Hartley, a Republican consultant in the state, told me. But he remains convinced that Ohio favors Republicans and that those Republicans listen to Trump: “If we turn our people out, we win.” But Husted’s choice to tether himself to the president does not guarantee success when 60 percent of Ohioans disapprove of Trump, up from 44 percent at the start of his current term. T rump is not the only one with an image problem in Ohio. It’s not hard to find prominent Democrats willing—eager, actually—to criticize their own party. And though Democratic self-flagellation is nothing new, what’s different in 2026 is that bashing their own party might be a winning strategy for Democrats in the state. Ohioans are not voting for Democrats “because they’re Democrats. They’re voting for them because we’re not Trump,” Tim Ryan, a former Democratic representative from the Youngstown area who lost a 2022 Senate race to J. D. Vance, told me. Allison Russo, a former minority leader in Ohio’s state house who is now running for secretary of state, says that the party’s organizing efforts in the state have been “terrible” and that the party’s brand is “crap.” But Russo, who still speaks with a southern drawl from her childhood in Mississippi, isn’t particularly beat up about that. “I would argue the Republican brand is becoming just as toxic,” Russo told me when we met in Upper Arlington, the Columbus suburb where she lives. She thinks she might win, which surprises even her. “What I thought my chances were at the beginning versus where we are now has shifted dramatically,” she said. A Democrat has not been elected Ohio secretary of state in 20 years. A decade ago, as Trump barreled toward his first term in the White House, then–First Lady Michelle Obama offered Democrats some advice on how to respond to his divisive brand of politics. It was, she said at the 2016 Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia, the Obamas’ family motto, a mantra of sorts that she and her husband would repeat to their young daughters as they grew up in the public eye: “When they go low, we go high.” Democrats grabbed onto the slogan, but the Obamas’ strategy of earnest, upbeat politicking did not help the party defeat Trump. In Ohio a decade later, Brown’s campaign all but repudiates the approach. When he tried to go high in the past, he “was shouted down by the ugly,” Diane Valentino, an elementary-school teacher in Delaware County, told me on the first day of early voting. She had arrived at the Delaware County Board of Elections before doors opened at 8 a.m., and stood with a small group of activists who were passing out Democratic flyers and sample ballots from the back of someone’s car. In this year’s election, Valentino felt, Brown had no choice but to “call out the darkness” of Ohio Republicans. “He didn’t strike first, but he had to step up,” Valentino said. [ Read: Jon Ossoff is doing something different ] After Brown cast his ballot that day in Columbus, he stopped to talk with a group of reporters. I asked him whether his campaign has a positive message to voters, or if tapping into frustration is the driving force heading into the final weeks of the campaign. “The positive message for my campaign,” Brown said, is, “I don’t see politics as left or right. I see it as whose side you’re on.” Not a Democrat—just on your side. Obama himself is the one massive exception to the “don’t remind people you’re a Democrat” strategy. This weekend, the former president will make his first visit to Ohio since 2018, the last time Brown won. When Obama announced that he would speak at a rally with Brown and Acton in Cleveland, he said that he wants to elect “Democrats up and down the ballot.” That includes Brown—just don’t expect him to say so.

items.title: The Man in the Middle of Trump’s Deeply Conflicted Ukraine Policy
items.description: D onald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky have never enjoyed a warm relationship, or even a stable one. But last week, it hit a new low. Trump called on the Ukrainian people to elect a new president, describing Zelensky as “more difficult to deal with” than Vladimir Putin. He accused Zelensky of prolonging Ukraine’s war with Russia. “He says he wants to settle, but he doesn’t,” Trump told Newsmax , without mentioning that it was Putin who started the war nearly five years ago. “Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with.” The two leaders may find themselves at a personal nadir, but all the while, the U.S. intelligence community has shown no letup in its fight to defend Ukraine against Russian aggression. Armed with information that the U.S. provides, Ukraine’s military has launched strikes deep inside Russia. And U.S. spy satellites provide early warning about incoming missiles and drones. Among U.S. personnel on the ground, “the CIA is in the lead,” a retired senior officer who travels frequently to Ukraine told me. If anything, the Ukrainians, with the CIA’s help, have gotten too good at hurting Russia for Trump’s taste. The administration’s policy is deeply conflicted, and perhaps no one understands that better than John Ratcliffe, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency. He has a foot in two worlds: advising a president who’s continuously at odds with Ukraine’s leadership, and running an agency that’s essential to Ukraine’s war for survival. One intelligence officer in the Baltics, who works closely with the Americans to counter Russian influence, told me that, though you’d never know it from Trump’s rhetoric, the CIA’s operations are now “much more aggressive” than they were during the Biden administration. The Ukrainians don’t see Ratcliffe as their advocate. They know he works for a mercurial boss, and that if Trump were to follow through on his recent threat to halt intelligence support unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian oil refineries, Ratcliffe would carry out the order. But Ratcliffe came into office promising, with Trump’s support, to return to the agency’s roots of espionage and clandestine operations. For now, that battlefield still extends to Ukraine. The CIA helped build the modern Ukrainian intelligence apparatus after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014. Partly owing to that long history, officials in Kyiv said they trust Ratcliffe to tell Trump the truth about the war, and not simply what the president wants to hear. More than a dozen current and former intelligence officials I spoke with in the U.S. and Europe described Ratcliffe, who served as the director of national intelligence in Trump’s first term, as clear-eyed about the threat Russia poses not just to Ukraine, but to the United States and its allies. (Most people shared their views on the condition of anonymity, to speak freely about the CIA director.) In that respect, Ratcliffe is not alone in the administration. Marco Rubio, when he ran for president in 2016, called Putin a “gangster and a thug.” And Pete Hegseth, when he was a television host, called him a “maniac” with ambitions to conquer Europe. But now, as senior Cabinet members with their own political ambitions, they have aligned themselves with the president’s rhetoric. Ratcliffe is a quieter adviser. He gives few interviews or speeches. He rarely posts on social media. Without needing to take a more conciliatory tone toward Moscow at press conferences and on cable, Ratcliffe is free to offer more candid advice in private. “He is well informed and understands the real situation,” one senior Ukrainian intelligence official who works directly with the CIA told me. “Their people stationed here support us very well. They are absolute professionals.” The official suggested that Ratcliffe would be a more effective peace negotiator than Trump’s current envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Ratcliffe, who declined my request for an interview, has shown no inclination to switch jobs. And why would he? He enjoys a rare position in Trumpland—always in the room and (so far) never on the outs. He spends many working hours at the White House. He and the president regularly play golf together. Ratcliffe has advised Trump on some of his most consequential foreign-policy decisions of the last two years, including the choice to go to war in Iran. [ Read: The rise of John Ratcliffe ] Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s first DNI during his second term, was so far removed from his inner circle that when the president was making final preparations to invade Venezuela, she was posting photos of herself from a beach in Hawaii. Ratcliffe was exasperated by Gabbard’s habit of stoking controversies and peddling conspiracy theories on social media, people who know them told me. Her most enduring contribution to national security was to gut the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, slashing the number of personnel by more than a third. As the ODNI has declined in size and relevance, the CIA, with Ratcliffe in charge, has reclaimed its traditional role at the center of the intelligence community. On paper, the president’s chief intelligence adviser is the director of national intelligence. In practice, it’s Ratcliffe. H ow much influence Ratcliffe , or any intelligence leader, actually has over Trump depends on the president’s willingness to listen. And that record is mixed. (Trump didn’t exactly heed their warnings about how Iran would respond to American attacks.) But people who’ve worked for Ratcliffe told me he believes that his job is to advise the president, not to make policy. He can explain the consequences of potential actions, as he did when he helped Trump weigh the costs and benefits of bombing Iranian nuclear facilities last year. Ratcliffe had said he believed Iran was hoarding nuclear material in order to make a weapon. But he did not, and will not, advocate that the president pick one approach over the other, people who have worked with him told me. In that respect, Ratcliffe has turned out to be like most of the CIA directors who preceded him. And that comes as some relief to skeptics—including inside the agency—who worried that he might follow the example of other top Trump officials who have vilified their employees or used their office to exacerbate culture wars. Elected to Congress from a deeply conservative Texas district in 2014, Ratcliffe got Trump’s attention during televised hearings about the FBI’s investigation of Russian election interference, which he suggested was motivated more by political animus than genuine concern about foreign-intelligence threats. He joined the Trump administration as DNI in 2020. Ratcliffe is still a Trump loyalist. But compared with Gabbard, Hegseth, or FBI Director Kash Patel, he is comparatively restrained in his criticism of the intelligence community, focusing mostly on Obama-era leaders and their alleged anti-Trump bias , instead of on his current employees. “I’ve always thought he was a workhorse, not a show horse,” a former official who worked with Ratcliffe told me. He doesn’t roam the halls of headquarters to chat with staff. In the early days of his tenure, his conspicuous absences from Langley and his constant presence at the White House made some CIA officers question where his priorities lay, current and former officials told me. But it’s not unusual for directors to covet face time with the president. And his relationship with Trump and low-profile manner have probably helped keep the president from attacking the agency. (Gina Haspel, a career CIA officer who served as director in Trump’s first term, successfully pursued the same strategy, current and former officials noted.) The CIA’s success in Ukraine has become a problem—at least from Trump’s perspective. Relentless attacks on Russian oil refineries have hobbled its economy and choked Putin’s war machine. The International Energy Agency estimates that in the first eight months of this year, Ukraine hit a refinery on average once every three days. Economists say that Iran’s restriction of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has driven up the cost of diesel. But Trump blames the damage to Russian refineries for the spiking prices, and he wants the Ukrainian attacks to end. On October 9, as officials from Kyiv and other European capitals met with Trump’s envoys in Miami for peace talks, the president announced that Putin had just agreed to start selling Russian diesel on the global market. With the midterms less than four weeks away, he sounded jubilant when he posted on Truth Social that diesel prices would be “COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump’s announcement surprised the negotiators, three people with knowledge of the talks told me. Some of his advisers had urged him to hold off on speaking with Putin until there was a concrete peace proposal for him to respond to, concluding that Trump would look weak if he relaxed sanctions but came away with no reciprocal commitments. Putin made none. Trump seemed to believe that dangling the prospect of fuel revenue to resuscitate Russia’s economy could bring Putin back to the table. But for years now, the U.S. intelligence community has assessed that Putin keeps fighting, despite an enormous loss of lives and money, because he thinks he will win—if not through an outright military victory, then by exhausting the support of Ukraine’s allies. To that end, Russia in recent months has escalated its “hybrid warfare” against Europe, plotting sabotage on commercial cargo aircraft, jamming communications, and probing NATO air defenses with drones. European intelligence officials told me they fear that Putin might even send forces across the border with Estonia, as he did in Crimea in 2014 when so-called little green men appeared, stripped of their military insignia. [ Read: NATO’s nightmare ] Back in August, Trump tried a subtler tactic to bring the war to a close. He dispatched Ratcliffe to Moscow, where he met with his counterparts in the security services and laid out the agency’s view about how the war was going, people familiar with the meeting told me. The upshot: No one was winning. Russia’s military has failed to make meaningful advances, but Ukraine has not expelled Russian forces from its territory. That’s hardly a secret analysis. But Ratcliffe’s presence sent a message of its own. The director was using a line of communication informally known as “the channel,” which allows Russian and American spies to talk candidly, away from the scrutiny of the press or the grandstanding of politicians. Putin, an ex-KGB officer, would understand that Ratcliffe had come not as a diplomatic envoy but as a fellow spy, with a message he felt was important for Putin to hear. Ratcliffe never met with Putin; that’s not how the channel works. But the Russian intelligence chiefs would have been obliged to document whatever the CIA director told them, even if they tried to dismiss it out of hand, a Western intelligence official told me. The U.S. and its allies have long suspected that Putin’s advisers may be misleading him about Russia’s chances of success in Ukraine. If Ratcliffe could help convince Putin that he was pursuing a lost cause, perhaps he’d finally come to the table. Among all the officials in the Trump administration, Ratcliffe was uniquely situated to deliver that message. No one knows the state of the war, and the stakes involved, better than the CIA officers who are working in Ukraine and monitoring the fight from headquarters. In September, Ratcliffe briefed Zelensky about his trip to Moscow when their planes were both in Ireland for refueling stops, a source familiar with the conversation told my colleague Simon Shuster. A U.S. official told me that the meeting took place entirely by happenstance. But it demonstrated the ability for Ukrainian leaders and the CIA director to have candid discussions on short notice. L ast week , Ukraine got a taste of what diminished U.S. intelligence support might look like. Russian missiles pounded Kyiv as reports emerged about disruptions to the Starlink satellite network and U.S. early-warning systems, which blinded Ukraine to some incoming Russian projectiles and limited its ability to intercept them, people familiar with the matter told me. The Ukrainian intelligence official said he blamed the Americans, but there’s also evidence that technical failures were responsible for the failure to intercept at least some of the incoming missiles. Officially, the Americans haven’t yet turned off the intelligence spigot, although Trump could act at any time. [ Read: Trump’s October surprise ] If Trump were to do so, people who have worked with Ratcliffe tell me that he wouldn’t lobby the president to change his mind, no matter the misgivings at CIA headquarters. At his confirmation hearing in 2025, Ratcliffe pledged to get the CIA back to what he considers its core mission. “We will conduct covert action at the direction of the president, going places no one else can go and doing things no one else can do,” he said, and told CIA officers listening that “if all of this sounds like what you signed up for, then buckle up and get ready to make a difference. If it doesn’t, then it’s time to find a new line of work.” Many people have taken Ratcliffe up on his suggestion. Although the CIA doesn’t disclose personnel figures, current and former officers told me they have never seen such a large number of retirements and resignations in their career. Some have even left on the verge of a major promotion. Vacancies in senior posts might have to be filled by less experienced officers. When CIA officers quit, their colleagues gather in the lobby of the headquarters building for a “clap out,” a round of applause to wish them well on their last day. Ratcliffe isn’t a fan of the tradition, two former employees told me. They serve as a reminder that many people have left. Ratcliffe also made decisions early in his tenure that some now-former officers told me they couldn’t condone. At his confirmation hearing, he warned that “a politically motivated, bureaucratically imposed social-justice agenda” risked distracting intelligence officers from their work. Once in office, he dismissed senior personnel who had been assigned to DEI-related roles. Former officials told me many of the people who were fired were simply unlucky enough to have been assigned those jobs while they waited for higher-level positions to open up, and were unfairly maligned as activists. He also fired about 60 probationary employees, who had less than two years’ experience. Some of them had already been put on notice that they were underperforming, but the mass termination still shocked many agency officers. This is not to say that everyone is unhappy at Langley. Broadly speaking, current and former officers told me, morale is highest in the operations directorate, among the officers who conduct the espionage that Ratcliffe wants to emphasize. Personnel in the Special Activities Center, which conducts covert and paramilitary activities, are particularly satisfied, recently retired officers told me, perhaps because they’re so busy, and not only in Ukraine. CIA directors don’t typically crow about secretive operations, but Ratcliffe has eagerly shared what he’s described as operational successes. In a speech last June, he said that “thanks to CIA,” U.S. special forces were able to locate and apprehend Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro “less than four minutes after their feet hit the ground on the largest military complex in that country.” (A senior Pentagon official told me that Ratcliffe took too much credit for the operation, but he didn’t deny that the agency’s contributions were important.) During the same speech, Ratcliffe credited the agency with helping locate a U.S. fighter pilot shot down over Iran, and for the “flawless intelligence picture” that had allowed more than 100 U.S. aircraft to hit Iranian nuclear facilities a year earlier. But some of the agency’s more opaque activities have stirred anxiety. Press reports have revealed CIA operations in Mexico and El Salvador as part of the Trump administration’s clandestine efforts to combat drug cartels. In August, The Washington Post reported that a series of air strikes targeting Ecuadorian fishing boats near the Galápagos Islands, a known hub for drug traffickers, were part of a covert CIA program. Legal experts have said that U.S. air strikes against boats suspected of carrying illegal drugs may violate the laws of armed conflict and in some cases could be considered murder. Recently retired officers told me that some of their colleagues have avoided taking jobs in the CIA’s Americas and Counternarcotics Mission Center. “There are people at the operational level who, when the Democrats take over the House, will be left holding the bag,” one former officer told me. “The agency is over its skis right now.” At the other end of the morale spectrum are employees in the analysis directorate, who write the articles, reports, and assessments that the president and his team use to make policy decisions. Since Ratcliffe became director in January 2025, significantly more analysts have reported concerns that the objectivity of their work is being undermined, according to an annual survey that I first reported on in July. The respondents directed most of their criticism at Gabbard, after she fired senior analysts who refused to alter their reports to support administration policy. But the results reflect a broader suspicion that the administration will reject information that it doesn’t want to hear. That will cause analysts to pull their punches, which in turn will deprive policy makers of the best advice, former analysts told me. Julia Curlee, who resigned in May as a senior CIA analyst, faulted Ratcliffe for not defending the agency officers whom Gabbard ordered be fired, and for rescinding or revising assessments that had been written before his tenure, after judging them to be politically biased. “Every officer drew the obvious conclusion: The director won’t protect even our most respected analysts when they tell hard truths, so they stopped telling them and learned to avoid topics the White House didn’t want to hear,” Curlee told me. “Ratcliffe isn’t protecting the CIA from politicization; he’s leading it.” [ From the October 2026 issue: The wrong kind of American ] A nalysts strive for objectivity . But intelligence as a practice is not truly apolitical, because it’s an instrument of presidential power. The most successful CIA directors know how to tell their bosses the truth while also serving their interests. Ratcliffe has largely managed to walk that fine line. Last year, he ordered analysts to reexamine what Trump calls “the Russia hoax,” the agency’s conclusion that Russia interfered in the 2016 election with the goal of helping Trump win. In public remarks, Ratcliffe said the review proved that Obama-era national-security leaders had created a “politically charged environment,” and he threw the credibility of their findings in doubt. But the CIA review, which Ratcliffe released, offered scant evidence to support that assertion, didn’t change the conclusion, and generally praised the quality of the CIA’s work. Over the summer, the agency declassified documents about China’s efforts to interfere in the 2020 election. In a prime-time national address , Trump said the intelligence was evidence of China’s malign actions and systemic weaknesses in the security of elections. But again, the documents didn’t support all of his claims. Ratcliffe issued a measured statement about backing Trump’s “transparency initiatives” that called out China’s interference, but he didn’t repeat the president’s assertion that the election was stolen. Election deniers close to the president have urged him to declare a national emergency and assert federal control over elections because of alleged foreign interference. With the midterms approaching, the two top Democrats on the intelligence oversight committees in the House and Senate said this week that they had put Ratcliffe on notice: If Trump claims publicly that the CIA gave him intelligence that a foreign power interfered in the election, the lawmakers will call Ratcliffe and ask if Trump is telling the truth. “You must be available to us on that day,” Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut told reporters. “So when the president makes that announcement, you will answer your cellphone to give us information about what’s happening.” Himes and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said Ratcliffe had promised to answer their call. Even when he has waded into political controversy, Ratcliffe has managed to shield the CIA from Trump’s ire. Considering that when the president came into office the first time he compared intelligence officers to Nazis, this is not an insignificant achievement. Ratcliffe also does a better job than most Cabinet members of explaining the president’s hasty decisions. Last year, when Trump abruptly cut off intelligence to Ukraine after his televised blowup with Zelensky in the Oval Office, Ratcliffe spoke about why the pause would probably be short-lived. “Trump had a real question about whether President Zelensky was committed to the peace process, and he said: Let’s pause ,” Ratcliffe told Fox Business five days after the leaders met. (That was a diplomatic summary. Trump had told Zelensky that he was disrespectful and ungrateful.) But after he left the White House, Zelensky sent Trump a note, which he also posted on social media, praising the president for his “strong leadership” and assuring him that “Ukraine is ready to come to the negotiating table.” “We do really value how much America has done to help Ukraine maintain its sovereignty and independence,” Zelensky said. Trump read portions of the note to a joint session of Congress, and called Zelensky’s conciliatory words “important.” Ratcliffe said that Trump’s pause had given time for Zelensky to consider his next move. The director clearly believed that the Ukrainian leader had made the right choice when he reached out to Trump, and he accurately predicted that the intelligence would start flowing again. “I think we’ll work shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine as we have to push back on the aggression that’s there, put the world in a better place for these peace negotiations to move forward,” he said. The CIA director seemed to be counseling Zelensky over the airwaves, a technique Trump’s own advisers have employed. The message came down to this: Remember who you’re dealing with, and things might work out. Ratcliffe might not advocate to his boss, but he knows how to read him. Simon Shuster contributed additional reporting. *Illustration sources: Brendan Smialowski / AFP / Getty; Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg / Getty; Daniel Slim / AFP / Getty; Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto / Reuters; Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool / AFP / Getty.

items.title: Commercialisation agricole : 105 milliards de FCFA mobilisés, 44 milliards d’arriérés à régler
items.description: Finalisation du financement de la SONACOS, règlement des arriérés dus aux fournisseurs d’intrants, paiement des producteurs et meilleure organisation des points de collecte : le Gouvernement a défini plusieurs mesures pour éviter les blocages de la précédente campagne et assurer le bon déroulement de l’exercice 2026-2027. À l’approche de la campagne de commercialisation agricole, le Gouvernement entend agir sur l’un des principaux facteurs de perturbation des filières : la disponibilité des financements au moment de la collecte. Réuni le 22 octobre 2026, le Conseil interministériel a fixé des mesures destinées à sécuriser les achats, à fluidifier les paiements et à préparer, dès maintenant, la prochaine campagne de production. La précédente campagne a enregistré des résultats significatifs. La SONACOS a collecté 219 171 tonnes d’arachides, générant 73,43 milliards de FCFA injectés dans le monde rural. Cette performance a été soutenue par une mobilisation financière de 105 milliards de FCFA, avec le concours de l’ITFC, de la BADEA, de la BOAD et du pool bancaire national. Ces acquis n’ont toutefois pas empêché des difficultés liées à la continuité des financements et à la faible utilisation des points de collecte agréés. Un financement à boucler avant la collecte Pour la campagne 2026-2027, le Gouvernement demande que le plan de financement de la SONACOS soit finalisé avant l’ouverture de la collecte arachidière, prévue à la fin du mois de novembre. L’entreprise devra également disposer d’une trésorerie de démarrage estimée à un milliard de FCFA par jour pendant les trente premiers jours, en attendant les premiers décaissements des bailleurs. Le Conseil interministériel a également retenu le règlement de 44 milliards de FCFA d’arriérés dus aux fournisseurs d’intrants. Sur la base des factures liquidées, chaque opérateur devra recevoir une attestation officielle de créance sur l’État. La mesure vise à traiter les engagements accumulés dans la filière et à faciliter la préparation des opérations à venir. Au-delà de ces engagements, un plan de financement opérationnel devra être arrêté avant l’ouverture de la campagne, filière par filière et selon les débouchés. Il devra sécuriser en priorité l’achat et le paiement des semences, indispensables à la prochaine production. Le dispositif prévoit notamment des garanties partielles du FONGIP pour les crédits de collecte, le recours aux récépissés d’entreposage et à la tierce détention, ainsi que des mécanismes de domiciliation des règlements. Des paiements mieux encadrés Les producteurs qui le souhaitent pourront être payés par mobile money, grâce à leur enrôlement sur la plateforme agro-sylvo-pastorale du Sénégal. L’objectif est de réduire les délais et les coûts de transaction. Le Gouvernement entend également adapter le nombre de points de collecte à la production attendue et aux financements réellement disponibles, après une campagne marquée par l’inactivité de plus des trois quarts des points agréés. Le coton fait aussi partie des priorités financières. Une enveloppe de soutien de 5 milliards de FCFA doit être confirmée avant le 15 novembre, date d’ouverture de la campagne. Le Gouvernement prévoit en outre de programmer l’apurement des arriérés de la SODEFITEX. Enfin, les autorités veulent anticiper les besoins de la campagne de production 2027-2028, en arrêtant son budget prévisionnel sans délai et en intégrant l’assurance agricole aux programmes publics d’intrants. Le Secrétariat général du Gouvernement devra présenter un état d’exécution des décisions avant l’ouverture de la collecte arachidière. C.G.D

items.title: The Gulf’s emerging web of security partnerships
items.description: The signing of the Badr Memorandum of Understanding by Pakistan, Türkiye, Qatar and Indonesia in Doha on Wednesday is the latest manifestation of Middle Eastern states accelerated efforts for diversifying their defense partnerships amid growing doubts about the reliability of existing security arrangements of the region led by the United States. But, rather than laying the foundations of a new regional security architecture, the proliferation of such agreements is producing a more fractured landscape in which countries are drawing in more partners, pursuing separate strategic interests and accepting varying levels of military commitments. There could not be a bigger example of how uneven is the process than the agreements being signed up by regional countries themselves. Badr , for instance, focuses on defense manufacturing, technology transfer, research and development, and training, allowing its participants to pool industrial capabilities without committing themselves to military assistance in the event of an attack. In contrast the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement , concluded in August by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye, goes considerably further by providing that an attack on one participant will be treated as an attack on all as it builds on a bilateral Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement between Pakistan and KSA signed in Sept 2025. These are two major agreements in addition to several others being signed or solidified by the countries in the region, but the contrast between Badr and Makkah agreements is telling because these agreements are often taken as evidence of an emerging regional security architecture, although the arrangements differ considerably in their purpose and obligations. Makkah agreement formalises security guarantees between participating countries, while Badr aims to develop industrial capacity. The momentum behind these regional security initiatives has grown since this year’s US - Israel war with Iran exposed the risks of relying heavily on external protection. For Gulf states in particular, the Iran conflict raised questions about whether existing security partnerships could adequately protect their interests during a major regional confrontation. Importantly, the response of the affected countries has not been to abandon US, whose military capabilities are still considered indispensable, but to seek additional options through new partnerships, domestic defense production and selective commitments. Besides the impression of the inadequacy of US security umbrella, this search for greater strategic autonomy also needs to be looked at in the context of the Gulf Cooperation Council’s own Joint Defense Agreement, signed in 2000, which too provides that aggression against one member constitutes aggression against all, yet the bloc has struggled to translate this commitment into an integrated military capability because of differences in equipment, command systems and national priorities. The hurdles to full operationalisation of Peninsula Shield Force has further exposed the gap between a collective defense principle and the ability to organise a coordinated response. The newer arrangements that the countries in the region are signing up partly reflect this GCC experience. Therefore, while these countries want enhanced security cooperation, they are also reluctant to surrender the freedom to make independent decisions. As a result, a network of partnerships is emerging that may complement one another in some areas without actually adding up to a common defense system. Pakistan’s expanding role illustrates both the opportunities and the limitations of this approach. Its relationship with Saudi Arabia has acquired a more formal security dimension through the 2025 bilateral agreement and the subsequent Makkah framework, while cooperation with Turkiye offers scope for closer military coordination and defense industrial collaboration. Egypt, another key player in the Arab world, has stayed outside the Makkah framework and has offered defense cooperation to Saudi Arabia, reflecting its interest in protecting its own regional priorities without becoming committed to a wider military confrontation. Islamabad’s other Gulf relationships, however, remain more limited in scope. Kuwait has strengthened defense cooperation with Pakistan through an upgraded agreement - the Protocol Agreement 2026 - covering training, capacity building and border management, while Bahrain has developed close links with the Pakistani military through the presence of Pakistani personnel in its National Guard and Coast Guard, alongside cooperation in training and logistics. These relationships have provided a basis for continued military engagement but do not carry the mutual defense obligations associated with the Pakistan - KSA partnership. Ties with UAE have, meanwhile, followed a more complicated course marred by political and financial strains, Islamabad’s closer alignment with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi’s expanding defense relationship with India. Nevertheless, training, personnel exchanges, counterterrorism activities and joint exercises between the two countries continue. Qatar has signed a defense industrial cooperation agreement involving Pakistan among others while Oman has maintained selective military ties with Pakistan and Turkiye, simultaneously preserving its wider security relationships and avoiding binding mutual defense commitments, consistent with its preference for neutrality and diplomatic engagement, particularly in relation to Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. This makes it difficult to describe Pakistan’s growing defense relationships as a unified regional bloc. Moreover, commitments under these agreements vary according to the interests and calculations of individual partners. Islamabad, in this situation, is left to balance closer security ties against its available military resources and the risk of becoming involved in conflicts whose objectives may not coincide with its own. At the same time the Gulf states are also pursuing different courses. Saudi Arabia is strengthening its relationships with Pakistan and Turkiye while continuing to rely on Western military capabilities and Egypt and exploring defense industrial cooperation with China. The UAE, which has not joined either the Makkah or Badr frameworks, has deepened security cooperation with Israel, including in air defense and counter drone capabilities, while maintaining close relationships with US, France and India. Qatar is seeking to expand its defense industrial partnerships through Badr but at the same time retains US military presence at Al Udeid. Bahrain remains closely aligned with Saudi Arabia and the GCC defense framework, while Kuwait continues to prioritise bilateral military cooperation with Pakistan alongside its substantial security relationship with Washington. Oman’s preference for neutrality and mediation further distinguishes its approach from those seeking more formal security commitments. The differences are not only confined to the choice of partners, but the states also have divergent assessments of the threat posed by Iran, the role of Israel in regional security and the degree to which they should commit themselves to one another’s defense. Their partnerships are therefore being shaped as much by the need to preserve freedom of action as by the desire to develop collective capabilities. The new partnerships do not either automatically translate into military independence for regional states, which continue to operate substantial inventories of Western origin aircraft, air defense systems and other advanced platforms that require specialised maintenance, software support, spare parts and replacement munitions. New partners may help diversify procurement and develop local production, but they cannot necessarily replace established suppliers on the required scale. Moreover, addition of newer systems can also complicate logistics and interoperability unless countries invest in common procedures, training and secure communications. Defense industrial cooperation presents another challenge and agreements such as Badr will acquire practical significance only if they lead to funded production programs, meaningful technology transfer and capabilities that participating countries can maintain and sustain. Similarly, the credibility of mutual defense arrangements will depend on whether their members can coordinate intelligence, plan jointly and establish procedures for responding to a crisis. The number of agreements signed, therefore, is less important than the military capabilities and obligations they actually produce. For Washington, this proliferation of new defense agreements may apparently look like a challenge, but this should definitely not be seen as it being replaced. US undoubtedly remains deeply embedded in the region through military bases, intelligence cooperation, arms sales and longstanding defense relationships. The emerging shift may, however, give the regional countries greater bargaining power with established suppliers, particularly as they press for domestic production, technology partnerships and greater control over maintenance and supply chains. To put it simply the emerging arrangements are an attempt to manage the uncertainty created by recent geo-political developments especially the receding US footprint rather than replace the existing system outright. The central contradiction in the Gulf countries response to the emerging situation, however, is that while these states are seeking greater security through a proliferation of partnerships, they remain unwilling, or unable, to reconcile their differences over the threats they face and the obligations they are prepared to assume.

items.title: Arachide, riz, coton : les filières agricoles au cœur du plan gouvernemental
items.description: Écoulement des stocks d’arachide, compétitivité du riz local, relance du coton et nouveaux débouchés pour les céréales et les produits horticoles : le Conseil interministériel du 22 octobre a arrêté des mesures spécifiques pour soutenir les différentes filières et améliorer la commercialisation des productions nationales. Le Gouvernement veut apporter des réponses différenciées aux difficultés rencontrées par les filières agricoles. Lors du Conseil interministériel consacré à la campagne 2026-2027, il a fixé des orientations allant de la valorisation des stocks à la régulation des importations, en passant par le financement des achats et l’organisation des circuits de commercialisation. Arachide : écouler les stocks et préparer la collecte Pour la filière arachidière, l’un des enjeux concerne les 70 450 tonnes de tourteaux détenues par la SONACOS. Le Gouvernement prévoit de diversifier les débouchés, notamment par la vente aux fabricants d’aliments pour bétail et aux meuniers, à un prix révisé. Une partie du stock doit également contribuer à l’assistance pastorale prévue pour la soudure 2026, dont les besoins en aliments de bétail sont estimés à 14 706 tonnes. La SONACOS est par ailleurs appelée à valoriser son patrimoine foncier afin de financer le renouvellement de ses anciennes lignes industrielles, de diversifier ses produits finis et de renforcer ses fonds propres. Pour la nouvelle campagne, le dispositif prévoit aussi un comité chargé de recommander chaque année un prix de l’arachide conciliant protection des producteurs et compétitivité à l’exportation. Riz local : améliorer l’écoulement et la compétitivité La situation du riz local appelle des mesures spécifiques. Au 13 octobre 2026, 13 879 tonnes de riz blanc avaient été enlevées sur un stock disponible de 41 729 tonnes. Le Gouvernement prévoit de mettre en œuvre un mécanisme de péréquation liant les importations aux achats de riz local et de payer aux riziers la subvention de 50 FCFA par kilogramme due sur les quantités déjà enlevées. Les autorités veulent également faire reconnaître l’interprofession réunissant producteurs, riziers et importateurs, sécuriser les stocks des rizeries grâce à la tierce détention et harmoniser les emballages, la qualité et la marque du riz local. Une stratégie de renforcement de sa compétitivité devra être élaborée avant la fin de l’année. Un atelier entre le Comité interprofessionnel riz du Sénégal et la Banque Agricole est aussi prévu avant l’ouverture de la campagne pour préparer le financement de 2027. Coton, maïs et productions diversifiées La relance du coton doit se poursuivre avec un objectif de production de 35 000 tonnes et un paiement des producteurs dans un délai de trois jours. L’enveloppe de soutien de 5 milliards de FCFA doit être confirmée avant le 15 novembre 2026. Le Gouvernement souhaite aussi associer des acheteurs industriels à la commercialisation et organiser la valorisation de la graine de coton par les huileries et les fabricants d’aliments pour bétail. Pour le maïs, le protocole entre l’État et les fabricants d’aliments pour bétail doit être renouvelé autour d’un objectif de 30 000 tonnes, avec un accompagnement bancaire. Dans l’horticulture, les autorisations d’importation seront liées à la disponibilité effective de la production nationale et à la justification d’achats locaux. Le fonds de commercialisation de l’oignon et de la pomme de terre doit être renforcé. Enfin, l’approche des protocoles de commercialisation sera étendue au mil et au sésame, avec des objectifs respectifs de 150 000 et 50 000 tonnes. Leurs besoins de financement devront être estimés et suivis chaque semaine, au même titre que ceux du riz local et des produits horticoles. À travers ces mesures, le Gouvernement cherche à mieux organiser les débouchés, à soutenir les producteurs et à réduire les difficultés d’écoulement des productions nationales. C.G. DIOP

items.title: Saint-Louis: l’Aser mise sur le solaire pour électrifier les villages isolés
items.description: En tournée à Saint-Louis, jeudi 22 octobre, le directeur général de l’Agence sénégalaise d’électrification rurale (Aser), Pape Momar Ngom a visité les installations solaires de Bouh Minguene et de Khelcom Diaw, dans la commune de Gandon. L’objectif est d’évaluer ces équipements et de renforcer les solutions d’accès à l’électricité dans les villages enclavés, en vue de l’électrification universelle à l’horizon 2029 Nommé le 1er octobre dernier, le nouveau directeur général de l’Aser a entamé sa tournée nationale par la région de Saint-Louis. Accompagné de représentants de Compagnie marroco-sénégalaise d'électricité (Comasel) concessionnaire de la zone, il a rencontré les populations pour recueillir leurs appréciations sur les installations solaires mises en place et identifier les difficultés rencontrées. Pape Momar Ngom a notamment salué l’intérêt des kits solaires individuels pour les localités où l’habitat est dispersé et où le raccordement au réseau électrique classique est coûteux. « Nous avons décidé de visiter ces installations pour voir comment démultiplier cette solution dans d’autres localités qui présentent des configurations similaires », a-t-il expliqué. Pour atteindre l’accès universel à l’électricité avant 2029, l’Aser prévoit trois approches notamment l’extension du réseau existant pour les villages proches des lignes électriques, la construction de centrales solaires avec un réseau de distribution pour les localités plus importantes et l’installation de kits individuels dans les villages les plus dispersés. 6 471 villages encore à électrifier et 400 milliards recherchés Ces équipements permettent notamment l’éclairage, la ventilation et l’utilisation de téléviseurs et de réfrigérateurs. Ils peuvent également améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage des élèves et faciliter la conservation des médicaments dans les structures sanitaires adaptées. « Les Sénégalais, où qu’ils se trouvent, ont droit à l’électricité », a affirmé le directeur général. Selon Pape Momar Ngom, 6 471 villages restent à couvrir dans le cadre des efforts engagés. Les besoins de financement sont estimés à 400 milliards de FCfa, en complément des projets en cours. Une table ronde avec les bailleurs a permis selon lui, de recueillir plus de 800 milliards de FCfa de promesses de financement, dont les conditions doivent encore être examinées. La tournée a également été marquée par une rencontre avec le préfet de Saint-Louis. Le directeur général a insisté sur la nécessité d’associer les autorités administratives à la mise en œuvre des programmes. « On ne peut pas faire des programmes de l’État sans passer par les autorités administratives », a-t-il souligné, rappelant que l’électricité constitue un service social de base essentiel à l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations rurales. Jeanne SAGNA (Correspondante)
